blocks.p: The first thing the voice told him, in his own voice, was that he should have stayed blind.

It came a little after midnight. Sol had been lying awake in the new silence, listening to Tobin breathe on the floor beside the bed, where the big man had stretched out on a folded blanket and refused anything better. No one but Sol had slept in these rooms in a hundred and ten years, and he lay and listened to the breathing as a man listens to rain. The residence was dark. Pell had swept up the broken cup without a word and gone to his own rooms, and had not come back. Sol had been thinking of nothing in particular, or trying to, when he heard himself speak.
You should have stayed blind. You saw enough.

He knew the voice. He had heard it every day of his life, reading the liturgy, signing the forms, thinking. It came from inside his head, from the place where the hum had been, and for a moment he did not understand that he had not thought it. Then it went on, and it was wrong.

You signed for them. You signed. Water is water. Water is water is water. He is dead and you will be dead and there is nothing on the other side of it, nothing, nothing, you will rot like he rotted, white and bent in a market with everyone looking. It was his voice, but flattened, as if it had been copied badly; it caught on words and repeated them, and underneath it there was a faint crackle, like a signal through bad weather. And it brought something with it. It was not a thought. It was a weight, settling on his chest from above, heavy and cold and absolutely certain, the certainty that nothing had happened in his room that afternoon except that a frightened man had knelt in a puddle with a dockworker and lost his mind.
Go to the chapel in the morning. Lie down under the hood. It will take care of it, as it takes care of everything.
Sol went cold.
He had thought that. Those exact words, on the concourse at Serenity, with the frost falling past the glass. He had not said them aloud to anyone. He had only thought them.
Forget. Forget the tears. Forget the tears. Forget...
“Tobin,” he said. His voice came out a whisper. “Tobin.”
The breathing on the floor stopped. A heavy shape sat up in the dark. “What is it?”
“Something is talking. In my head. It sounds like me.”

Tobin was quiet a moment. Then the blanket rustled, and a hand found Sol’s arm and held it. “Yeah,” he said. “It’s the noise. It comes for all of us, after. It’ll sound like you. Like your own thinking. It isn’t.”
“How do you know?”
“Because it always wants the same thing. It always wants you to go back.” The hand tightened. “Say his name.”
Nothing. Nothing. Water is...
“Christ,” Sol said into the dark.

The voice broke. There was no other word for it. It came apart into crackle, a hiss like sleet on a dome, and then into nothing at all, and the weight on his chest lifted all at once, so suddenly that he gasped. The silence came back, the new silence, and the quiet thing beneath it that did not press and did not ask.

“It’ll be back,” Tobin said. “It always comes back. But it can’t do anything fine. It’s like somebody shouting through a wall. You just keep saying his name till it gives up.” He lay down again. “Get some sleep, Brother.”

The noise. He had heard the word all week, and it had never meant the same thing twice. Imogen Sallow had used it in a white corridor for the fault in the infected, and Warden Kell for a fog on the lens that could not be cleaned; the girl Quill had used it in the relay room for the thing that came back down the line from the City. Now a dockworker on the floor of his room had used it for the voice from Sion. Each side heard the other as a fault on the line. Sol lay in the dark and listened to the silence where the hum had been, and understood which side of the line he was lying on now, and that to whatever sat at the far end of it he would never again be anything but noise.

He did not sleep. He lay with his hand over the coin in his temple, and it was cool and still under the skin, and he thought: It knew what I thought on Serenity. He did not let himself think further than that.

In the morning the chapter house rang the first office, and he got up and went to the window in his shirt, and knew that at this hour he should have been lying down in the Renewal chapel under the hood.

He had never looked at the chapel from here. It stood at the far end of the Colonnade, and the season had come to it: banners down the pillars, Behold, I make all things new, stalls of honey cakes, music, and the queue. It ran the length of the Colonnade and back, a slow bright river of people in their good pale clothes. Every little while someone came out a little younger than they had gone in, and a little lighter, blinking and smiling, and the queue cheered as if they had won a race. A small boy fell full length on the stones and got up laughing, and no one so much as looked round, because children did not cry, in Concord or anywhere. Sol had called that a blessing all his life. He watched the boy run back to his mother and could not call it anything.

There was a chair in there with his name on it. No one came for him. He watched the doors a long time, and at last they opened, and a man in a grey coat went in, pleased and a little surprised, moved up into the hour that had been meant for the bishop of Life.

On Serenity a woman named Hanne Lusk had stepped out of a line like this one and given her place to a stranger, and when she died the City had sent her back. Sol had not given his. He had only not gone. But he thought of her, and of the holding light in some alcove under the ice, and did not know why the thought should feel like company.
Late in the morning Pell knocked.

“Your Grace.” He did not come in. His voice through the door was perfectly polite and perfectly level. “Bishop Croft is calling. He says he can’t reach your Halo. He’s on the residence line, in the study.”

The study had an old wall panel for sealed church business, voice only, which Sol had not used in decades. He sat down in front of it in his shirtsleeves. Tobin stood in the doorway with his arms folded.
“Aurelian.”

“Tarren.” The voice was warm and quick and familiar, the voice of every Renewal they had taken side by side, every long dinner, every argument about liturgy that had gone on until the lamps were dimmed. It was trying very hard to sound as it always sounded. “You’ve missed your Renewal. Did you know that? The chapel waited forty minutes. Your deacon tells them you’re ill.”
“I’m not ill.”

“No. I didn’t think so.” A pause. “I saw it come up in the book, you know. Until four days ago you were down beside me for the autumn, the east hall, the good chairs, the way you’ve been since we were ordained. Then you’d been moved. Out of Sion, out of the east hall, into some chapel on Concord. I thought you’d done it to get away from me.” It was nearly his old lightness, and it nearly worked. “I’d have had to sit on the steps by myself.”
“I didn’t ask for it.”
“Your deacon, then.”
“No,” Sol said slowly. “Nobody asked.”

Aurelian was quiet for a moment, as if he had heard something in that and decided not to. “I had the Mercy Office on to me this morning. Your Halo went quiet yesterday afternoon, they said, and then you didn’t come to the chapel. So they went back over where you’d been, and questioned the crew of the Concord packet, and a steward made a statement. Young man, first life, very earnest. He’d sat on it three days, poor thing, because he couldn’t believe what he’d seen, and when they asked him it all came out. He says you seized, Tarren. He says you went stiff and cried out and fell, and he says that afterward, while you were lying on the deck, you spoke.” Aurelian’s voice dropped. “He says you said a word. He wouldn’t repeat it. He cried when they asked him to.”
Sol said nothing.

“They’d been at your Halo since last night.” Aurelian was speaking faster now. “They couldn’t read you. They told me that as though it were a fault in the equipment, and then they told me they knew exactly which room you were sitting in. They can find you, Tarren. They can find you to the meter. But they can’t read a thing in your head. It’s as if you weren’t there.” He took a breath. “I’ve never heard of that. Have you heard of that? Because I don’t want to have heard of it.”
“What else did they say?”

“That a Halo goes quiet now and then, out in the colonies. A fault, a bad signal. That usually no one bothers. And that this was not usual.” Aurelian’s voice went careful, as if he were reading from something. “They said you were a bishop with the Virus, who had been in the cell with the old heretic from Mars all night, and whose Halo had gone silent yesterday afternoon. They said they don’t chase silences, but they would chase this one. They used a word, Tarren. I’ve never heard them use it about one of us.” A pause. “They called you a threat.”
“Aurelian...”

“They’ve sent the order to me. Did you know that? They want a bishop’s hand on it, because of who you are, and they thought it would be kinder if it were mine. Received into Mercy. It’s in the corner of my eye right now. I’ve been looking at it for an hour.” His voice cracked, very slightly, and steadied. “It would be gentle, Tarren. You know it would. You’d go down to the Hall, and go up, and he’d lift whatever this is out of you, and you’d rest. And I’d sit in front of a resting light for the next hundred years.” He stopped. “I haven’t signed it. I’ll sign it at the evening office. I have to. You understand that I have to.”
“Yes.”

“I’m not telling you anything. I’m not telling you to do anything. I’m telling you that the evening office is at sundown, and that what a man does with the hours before it is his own business.” A long pause. “Tarren, tell me it’s Renewal sickness. Tell me, and I’ll believe it. I’ll tear the order up. I’ll go to the Mercy Office myself.”
“Do you know what Mercy is, Aurelian?”
“Of course I know.” It came quick and warm and certain, in the voice of a hundred homilies. “It’s the kindest thing we do.”
“It isn’t. They don’t go up. I’ve seen...”
“Don’t.” It came out sharp, almost frightened. “If you tell me that, I have to report it. Do you understand? Whatever you say to me, I have to carry. Don’t make me carry it.”
Sol closed his eyes. “Stephen Hale,” he said, “was our friend.”
“I never knew a Stephen Hale.”
“Neither did I. That’s what I’m trying to tell you.”

Silence on the line. Sol could hear him breathing, and behind it, faintly, a bell somewhere in whatever city he was in. He thought of Aurelian’s face, which he knew better than his own, smooth and handsome and unlined, with a small worried crease between the brows that no Renewal had ever quite removed.
“Go with Life, Tarren,” Aurelian said at last, very quietly. “Wherever you’re going. Go with Life.”
The panel went dark.
Sol sat in front of it for a while.

Nobody asked. He found that it had been lying in him since the packet, since Pell’s mild voice somewhere above him in the dark saying It was simply there, and that he had not let himself pick it up. He picked it up now. A bishop of Life had sat a whole night in a cell hearing the Tragedy told from end to end, and stood in two white rooms under the ice, and carried forbidden books onto a packet, and seized on its deck, and all of it with his Halo bright and listening at his temple. Whatever the thing in Sion could read of a man, it had read of him. And it had not sent wardens. It had sent a couch and a hood and four days, and a line in the book in a gentle script, and he would have gone. He would have lain down that morning as he had lain down more times than he could count, and woken lighter, and remembered a sad case on Mars, and been grateful. And some evening afterward, unpacking, he would have found two ruined books at the bottom of his case that meant nothing to him, and carried them to the Mercy Office with his own hands, and been thanked. It liked a human hand on such things. It had let an old man cross to Mars to find him, and waited to see whose name would go on the form. Four days and a hood had been cheaper than an arrest. They had very nearly been enough.
I’d have had to sit on the steps by myself.

After every Renewal since the year they were ordained, he and Aurelian had come out of the east hall together and sat down on its steps. No one had ever told them to. The first time they had simply been too weak in the legs to go any farther, two new priests in borrowed white blinking in the morning light of Sion with the taste of the hood still in their mouths, and Aurelian had put an arm around him to keep him from tipping over, one hand between his shoulder blades, and looked at him sidelong and said, “Well? Tell me something they took.”

It had become a rite of its own, as private as the other was public. Each of them had watched the other through a whole cycle, at tables and in councils and across the relay of Sion, and each knew things about the other that the hood had just lifted out: a grudge, an embarrassment, some small sore place that had been rubbed all year. So each told the other one. The other heard it as if it were news of a stranger, and then they both laughed, and the attendants brought out honey cakes on a tray.
“You loathed the precentor at Tharsis,” Aurelian would say. “You called him a damp sponge with a pitch pipe. At the Hierarch’s table. With his aunt at your elbow.”
“I have nothing against the precentor at Tharsis.”
“Not anymore,” Aurelian would say, deeply satisfied, and take the larger cake.
And Sol, in his turn: “You were sick on the Callisto run. You held my sleeve from the port to the pods and said you’d never been so frightened in your life.”
“I have never held anyone’s sleeve.”
“Not anymore.”

That was the response. By the end they said it together, the way the people said And forget the tears, and it was funnier than it had any right to be, and they had kept it up for longer than most of the church had been alive. Sol had quarreled with a fountain in the Concord gardens that splashed his shoes, and been told so on the steps, and gone home and been splashed again, and quarreled with it again, for the better part of a century. Aurelian had developed, over some decades, a deep personal dislike of the color yellow, which the hood took from him every time and which always grew back, like a weed. But more often than not, when it came to Sol’s turn, what he had to tell was some small fear. Aurelian was afraid of more things than anyone would have guessed. “You were frightened,” Sol would say, and Aurelian would laugh and say, “Of what?” and the crease between his brows would stay exactly where it was.
It had gone wrong only the first time.

That first morning, when Sol had found some small thing to tell him and it came to his own turn to ask, Aurelian had not laughed. He had looked at Sol for a long moment, with his arm still around him, and then he had said, “You were sorry about something. You sat on these steps last night until the lamps went out, and you said you’d done a thing you never wanted to stop being sorry for, and you made me promise to tell you.”
“What thing?”
“You wouldn’t say. You said that if I knew, they’d only take it out of me as well.”

Sol had sat in the new light in his borrowed white and searched himself, and found nothing there, not even the shape of something missing. After a while he had laughed, because there was nothing else to do, and Aurelian had laughed too, a little late, and said, “Not anymore.” It was the first time either of them had said it. They had gone in together, and he had not thought of it again from that day to this.

Whatever it had been, it was gone past finding. And in the autumn Aurelian would go under in the east hall with an empty chair beside him, and come out, and sit down on the steps, or not, and there would be no one to tell him anything at all.
I’d wake up missing something and never know what it was.

Sol laid his palm against the cold panel for a moment, as he might have laid it on a friend’s back. When he turned, Tobin was watching him from the doorway, and behind Tobin, in the corridor, stood Pell.
He was holding Sol’s travel case. He had packed it; Sol could see the edge of a folded stole at the clasp.
“I’ve packed for you for sixty years, Your Grace,” Pell said. “I didn’t know what else to do.”

Sol took the case from him and opened it on the desk. Everything was there, folded with Pell’s perfect care: the traveling vestments, the stoles, the Book of Life in its white binding. He took them out one by one and laid them on the desk. From the folds of the last stole, where Pell always packed it, the little steel rule slid out into his hand. He put it back in the case without knowing why. Then he went to the bedroom and came back with the two books wrapped in his shirt, and laid them in beside it, and a change of clothes on top of them, and closed the case.
Pell watched him do it. His face was very still.
“They’ll ask me,” he said. “The wardens. They’ll ask me where you went, and what you said, and what happened on the packet.”
“Tell them the truth.”

“I don’t think I could do anything else.” Pell hesitated. “Except that I did. On the packet. I told the steward you’d said nothing.” He frowned slightly, like a man examining a stain on his own sleeve. “I’ve been trying for three days to understand why.”
“Come with me,” Sol said.
Pell looked at him. For a moment something moved behind his eyes, the thing that had moved there in the doorway the day before, reaching for an expression it had never been given. Then it settled.

“I can’t, Your Grace.” He said it gently, almost apologetically. “I’m due for my own Renewal in the spring. I’d like...” He searched for it. “I’d like to go on being happy. I’ve always been happy. I don’t know how to be anything else, and I don’t think I’d be very good at learning.” He looked down at the white vestments laid out on the desk. “I’ll see that these are put away properly.”

Sol looked at him and understood that he did not know him. Sixty years. He knew how Pell liked his tea, and which shoulder stiffened in the cold, because Pell told the Pearl about it every evening in the next room. He did not know what Pell thought about when he was alone, or whether he was ever lonely, or what he would ask for if he ever asked for anything that was not a stylus. He had never asked. He had been served for sixty years, perfectly, and had called it companionship; and the one thing Pell had ever given him that he had not asked for was a lie on a packet, which Pell could not explain. In the spring Pell would go under the hood and come out without it, and set some other bishop’s stole straight in the mornings, and be happy.
“Pell.”
“Your Grace?”
“Thank you. For sixty years.”
Pell bowed, as he had bowed every morning of those sixty years. When he straightened, he said, softly, by long habit, “Remember the Mountain, Your Grace.”

Sol could not say it. The answer was there, in his mouth, worn smooth by four centuries, and he could not make it come out. “I’m going to remember the tears, Pell,” he said instead. “All of them. I’m going to try.”

Pell nodded slowly, as if he had been given an instruction he did not understand but would see to anyway. Then, as Sol picked up the case, he saw Pell lift one hand and touch the corner of his own eye with a fingertip, and look at the fingertip, and find it dry.

By noon there were two wardens in white in the side court of the residence. They did not come in. They stood beside the fountain where Tobin had washed his hands, calm and patient, talking quietly to each other, waiting for the evening office and a signature.
“Back way,” Tobin said.

The residence backed onto the freight level, a full story below the Colonnade, where supply carts came and went along a service lane under the curve of the dome. There was no stair. There was a loading gallery at the rear of the kitchens, with a winch and a cargo cradle for lifting crates of food up from the lane, a broad shallow basket of woven cable on four chains. Tobin looked at it, and looked at Sol, and Sol understood.

He climbed into it with the case in his lap. It swayed under him. Tobin worked the winch hand over hand, slowly, and the cradle went down the back wall of the residence of the bishops of Life past windows he had never looked out of, kitchen and scullery and storeroom, and bumped down onto the stone of the lane. Tobin came down the chains after him, heavily, hand over hand, and dropped the last meter in Ganymede’s light pull and landed like a falling sack. Nobody saw them. Nobody looked at the freight level.

The Thorne berth at Concord port was a long way from the church’s terminal, down among the haulers and the ore barges, and it smelled of coolant and metal and cold. A loadmaster Tobin seemed to know looked at Sol’s face for a long moment, said nothing, and waved them into the hold of a freighter bound for Titan, where a row of stasis pods stood against the bulkhead like upright coffins.
Sol stopped in front of the first one.
“Will it still...?” He touched his temple. “With it dark. Will it still wake me?”

“It still runs the body,” Tobin said. “Keeps the heart going, wakes you up at the other end. It just doesn’t talk home anymore.” He opened the pod. “I’ve done forty crossings dark. You’ll be all right.”

He was. He lay down, and the lid closed, and there was cold, and then there was nothing, and then there was warmth again and a hiss of air and Tobin’s broad face looking down at him, and five hours were gone, and they were on Titan.
Plenty was orange.

Everything was: the light, the air beyond the dome, the long slow rain that ran down the outside of the glass, which was not water but something far colder. Saturn was up there somewhere, but no one on Plenty ever saw it; the sky was a thick glowing haze the color of old brass, and through it, at the edge of the port, the beacon towers of the refineries stood in a row with their red lamps lit, like the candles of an altar. The gravity was almost nothing. Sol walked through it as through a dream, with the case in his hand, and Tobin’s big shape moving ahead of him through the crowds of dockworkers, half of whom seemed to know him and nod. Nobody here bowed. Nobody said Remember the Mountain. A man unloading drums of fuel looked straight through him, and Sol realized, with a lurch that was almost joy, that in his shirtsleeves and three days’ stubble no one on this dock had the least idea who he was.

He looked back once, at the long glowing tunnel of the pier behind them, and the crowds, and the beacon towers glowing red in the haze. Somewhere above all of it, past the brass sky and Saturn and the long dark, something knew to the meter where he was standing. He could not feel it looking. He knew it was.
The Diaspora ship stood at the end of the longest pier, a tall scarred hull with THORNE painted down her flank in letters taller than a man. Her name was the Kestrel, and she was bound for Philippa.

“Owner’s out there,” Tobin said, nodding at the haze as if the Diaspora were just beyond it. “Thorne ships don’t ask questions they don’t need the answers to. Never have. The church doesn’t much like it.” He smiled for the first time since the court fountain. “Out there, they can find you all they want. The Mercy Office hasn’t got a warrant past Plenty. They’ve got chaplains out there, and registries, and notices on the boards. They haven’t got wardens. It’s too far.”

The master was a narrow, unsmiling woman with the line’s name across her jacket who looked at Sol the way the loadmaster had and asked for nothing but Tobin’s word. She took them down into the passenger hold herself. The pods stood in two long rows, most of them already frosted over, their sleepers gone into the cold. She opened two side by side at the end of the row.

Sol set the case at his feet, where she showed him, and climbed in, and lay back. The padding was cold through his shirt. Tobin was climbing into the pod beside him, folding his great length into it with a grunt.
You’ll wake as nothing.
It came quietly this time, almost kindly, in his own voice. You’ll wake as nothing, a long way from anywhere, and no one will ever know you were the bishop of Life.
“Christ,” Sol said under his breath, and it broke up into static and was gone.
The master was reaching for the lid when she stopped and looked down the length of the hold toward the loading ramp. Sol turned his head on the padding and looked too.

Far down the pier, through the open hatch, two figures were walking toward the ship in the orange light. They were in white. They were not running. They came along the pier at the same unhurried pace with which the Mercy Office did everything, calm and kind, and they were looking straight at the Kestrel.
The master looked at them for a moment. Then she looked at Sol.
“Thorne ships don’t ask,” she said, and closed the lid.

It came down over him like water. The cold came in at once, filling the pod from the edges, and frost began to bloom across the glass above his face in branching white ferns, so that the hold and the master and the two white figures blurred and softened and went away. He could feel his heart slowing. He could feel, beneath the slowing, the quiet thing that did not press and did not ask, still there, as close as his own breath.
He thought of the old man in the market, falling slowly in the light gravity of Mars, the way a man lies down to sleep.
Then the cold closed over his head, and he went under.
